title: Building a design system with an AI team: tokens, a tested kit and a review loop on my phone
summary: toonish-ui is the comic-book component kit behind this site. It builds from one token file, fails CI when its output is stale, and took its look from rounds of me rejecting what Claude drew first.

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: My portfolio is a stack of case studies, and every one has the same parts: figures, tables, screenshots, a pull-request trail. I wanted those parts to look like one product, not like pages that happened to share a stylesheet. I also wanted the look to be mine, so I did not start from a template.

I do not draw, and I work with AI agents, so the real question was how to get a distinct, consistent design out of a team that has no taste of its own. The answer was to make the taste explicit. Tokens hold the decisions, tests hold the rules, and I hold the veto.

My design coursework at Full Sail University and my year at Apple taught me why this matters. UX and UI are not polish added at the end. They decide whether a person can use the thing, and that includes people who use a screen reader, a keyboard or a switch, not only people who tap a phone. That is why the kit has a mobile-first rule, a contrast test and, since I made it a hard rule, an accessibility standard.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: The kit is called toonish-ui and lives in [its own public repository](https://github.com/PeteDio-Labs/toonish-ui) under an MIT license. It began inside the portfolio repository and moved out once a second page needed the same parts. Every color, type size, space, radius, shadow and easing is in one file, `tokens/toonish.tokens.json`, in the W3C design tokens format. A build script turns that file into CSS variables, a Tailwind v3 preset, a Tailwind v4 theme and plain JSON. Nobody edits those four outputs by hand.

On top of the tokens sit the components, written as plain CSS so they work without Tailwind: buttons, cards, modals, a screenshot frame, data tiles, rows, stacked bars, a table for words, a card deck for phones, a pager, a portrait on a vector backdrop and the sound-effect lettering on the home page. A small script handles modals, toggle groups and the deck, with no framework. Helper functions in TypeScript return the markup for the parts that need it, and each one escapes every string it receives.

The look is blue, red, yellow and violet on deep navy, with cool grey paper panels, ink outlines two pixels thick and hard four-pixel shadows. Text is IBM Plex Sans and Plex Mono, and Bangers is the comic face for the logo, the hero and the sound effects. Every fill carries ink text, which keeps contrast at 5.1:1 or better, and a test computes that ratio on every run.

People should be able to use this site no matter who they are, so accessibility is a rule of the kit, not a feature of it. Components start from the right HTML element: a native `dialog` for the modal, real buttons and links, headings in order. ARIA roles and labels ship inside the components, so a site that uses the kit gets them without remembering to add them. The target is WCAG 2.2 AA. Some of this was already true: the modal is a native dialog, the deck is a labelled carousel with a live counter and inert background cards, decoration is hidden from screen readers, and motion stops under a reduced-motion setting. The rule makes it a standard to meet and to check.

sections.heading: How the kit stays correct
paragraphs: The repository commits its built `dist/` folder, because Bun does not run a dependency's build scripts, so a consumer can install straight from git. That creates a risk: the source and the committed output can disagree. The CI check rebuilds `dist/` and fails when it differs from the commit, and it names the files that changed. A build that matches no component classes also fails, so an empty stylesheet cannot pass.

Four checks run on every pull request: typecheck, build with the stale-output test, unit tests and a Chromium check at 1280 and 390 pixels. The browser check asserts computed styles, fonts, overflow, the modal, the toggle, reduced motion and console errors. It does not compare screenshots, because font rendering differs between machines, and it prints how many checks it ran, so a green result says what it examined.

Two rulesets guard the repository. The `main` branch takes changes only through a pull request with the check passing, and a `v*` tag can be created but never moved or deleted, so a released version cannot change under a consumer. A release is cut only when a consumer needs one, and the workflow checks that the tag, `package.json` and the changelog agree before it attaches a tarball and checksums.

The rule has to fail a build or it is only a hope, so the kit's CI is being extended to fail on accessibility regressions. That enforcement is in progress as I write this, and I have not yet counted its checks, so this study states no figure for it. Until it lands, the contrast test and the browser check are the only automated accessibility checks, and neither replaces testing with a screen reader and a keyboard.

sections.heading: How it ships
paragraphs: The portfolio installs the kit from an exact commit, not from a branch and not from a moving tag, so a kit change reaches the site only when I move the pin in a pull request. The site build copies the kit's stylesheet, script and fonts into the output, so no page loads either from a third party.

The site has two branches with two jobs. A change to the case studies goes to `main` by pull request. A change to the look goes to a `staging` branch first. A staging copy of the site, behind a login, builds that branch automatically, and I review it on my phone. When I say "send it", a pull request promotes staging to `main`. A workflow merges `main` back into `staging` after every push, with a merge commit and no force push, and fails loudly when the two conflict.

A push to `main` runs the tests, builds the pages, syncs them to a private S3 bucket and invalidates CloudFront, then waits for the invalidation and requests the home page, the study index and every study. It fails on any answer but 200. [The earlier study on how this site is built](https://pdlab.dev/work/how-this-site-is-built.html) covers the bucket, the headers policy and the deploy identity.

sections.heading: What went wrong
paragraphs: The first designs were wrong in ways I could see and Claude could not. The agents produced competent, forgettable pages, and I rejected the palette twice and the lettering once in a single afternoon. The fix was not a better prompt. It was writing each rejection into the repository: a brand brief that says which choices are closed, and a standing rule that I do not reopen them.

My desktop checks passed while my phone failed. A row of cards scrolled sideways, and my thumb got stuck in it on a real device. The kit now has a mobile-first rule in its README and its agent instructions: design at 390 pixels first, never add a sideways scroll container beyond the table wrapper, and keep decoration visible on a phone. The browser check fails when the page is wider than the screen at either width.

Some of it is still unproven. The Tailwind v4 theme builds from the tokens but I have not tested it against a real v4 project, and the changelog says so. The swipe deck passed in Chromium, and I have not confirmed it on every iOS version. The kit has no automated check that a component looks right, only that its computed styles and behavior are right, and it has two releases, not a track record.

sections.heading: Result
paragraphs: The site and the kit move independently. I can change a token, build, and see every component in the kit's own test fixture change together, and a stale build cannot reach `main`. New case studies use the kit's data components, so a table, a figure row or a screenshot looks the same in every study.

The part I would reuse anywhere is the loop, not the colors. An AI team proposes, I reject on a phone in seconds, the rejection becomes a token, a rule or a test, and the next proposal starts from there. The design system is the written-down version of my taste.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: Make the design decisions machine-readable and the rules testable, then let agents work inside them. Accessibility is one of those rules: write it as a standard, build it into the components and make CI fail without it. Review on the device your audience uses, because that is where the faults show. Write every rejection down once, so nobody has to make it again.
